questions.q: What is the difference between an SLI and an SLO?
options: They are two names for exactly the same thing
An SLI is the actual measured metric; an SLO is the internal target set for that metric
An SLI is external and contractual; an SLO is purely internal and has no target
An SLO is only used for CPU services, never for GPU inference
questions.explain: The SLI is the raw measurement (e.g., p99 TTFT); the SLO is the target value chosen for that measurement (e.g., 'p99 TTFT under 500ms').

questions.q: Why is an SLA typically set looser than the internal SLO?
options: To leave margin, since the SLA is an external, often contractual commitment with consequences if missed
Because SLAs are always stricter than SLOs by definition
SLAs and SLOs must always be numerically identical
SLAs only apply to free-tier customers
questions.explain: Teams typically set the external SLA looser than their internal SLO so there's margin to catch and fix problems internally before an external, contractual commitment is actually breached.

questions.q: Why should an inference SLO be defined using a percentile (like p99) rather than an average?
options: Percentiles are impossible to measure in production
An average can look fine while a real share of users experience far worse latency, since the average doesn't see the tail
Averages are always higher than percentiles
Percentiles only apply to throughput, never latency
questions.explain: A percentile target like p99 TTFT under 500ms directly bounds how bad the worst-affected requests can be, which an average can completely hide.

options: The amount of money allocated to fix bugs
The allowed share of requests that can miss the SLO before reliability work must take priority over other changes
A budget for buying additional GPUs
The maximum number of errors a developer can make per day
questions.explain: If an SLO targets 99.9% success, the remaining 0.1% is the error budget — a deliberate, pre-approved allowance that governs how much risk (deploys, experiments) a team can reasonably take.

questions.q: Why should an inference SLO be set against realistic, loaded traffic rather than a single quiet benchmark run?
options: Quiet benchmark runs always produce the most pessimistic numbers
An SLO set from a lightly-loaded test will likely be missed constantly once real concurrent production traffic arrives
Realistic load testing is illegal in most jurisdictions
SLOs don't need to be based on any measurement at all
questions.explain: Performance under light, quiet conditions is typically much better than under real concurrent load, so an SLO calibrated only from a quiet run sets an unrealistic target that production will routinely fail to meet.
